chunks: Buck at 100% and 0% duty. The question: What happens at 100% and 0% duty cycle?
At 100 percent duty the main switch never turns off, so the output is just the input minus a small drop. At 0 percent it never turns on, so nothing feeds the output.
In both cases the converter cannot regulate any more, because it has hit the end of its control range.
Think of a bathtub tap. At 100 percent it is fully open, so the tub just follows the supply and you have no control.
At 0 percent it is fully closed, so nothing arrives and the tub slowly drains through the plughole. All the fine control happens in between, when the tap flicks on and off.
Above V in equals 3. 52 volts the loop holds 3. 3 volts by choosing D<1 . Below that, D is stuck at its maximum and V out follows V in minus 0. 22 volts.
Regulation is lost, so any ripple or sag on V in goes straight to the load.
Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the switch is on ("What is duty cycle"). Dropout: how far below the input the output sits when the switch stays on.
Bootstrap capacitor: a small capacitor that supplies the extra voltage needed to hold the top (high-side) transistor on ("High-side NFET vs PFET trade-offs").
Minimum off-time: a short off period that controllers force so the bootstrap capacitor can recharge. Regulation: holding the output at its target value.
A buck has 5 volts in, runs at 100 percent duty and delivers 2 amps. The switch and inductor add up to 110 milliohms, so the drop is 2 times 0. 11 equals 0.
22 volts and the output is about 4. 78 volts. It tracks the input and cannot hold a lower target. That is the whole idea.

"At 100 percent duty the high-side is always on, there's no switching or ripple, and V out is the input minus the drops across the switch and inductor, so the converter is in dropout and not regulating.

At 0 percent the high-side is always off, the inductor current ramps down at V out over L , and the output decays; in a forced-PWM synchronous buck the current even reverses and feeds energy back to the input.
In real parts, bootstrap refresh and minimum on and off times keep the duty cycle away from both extremes."
